title: the birth
hook: a wedding procession, a brother driving the bride's chariot, and a voice from the sky that turns him into a killer
carry: a promise made at sword point

segments.voice: Yesterday the Pandavas' last journey ended in heaven, after Yudhishthira chose to stand in the dark beside his family. Your line was he will stay in hell. That closes the Mahabharata serial. Today a new book opens, the Bhagavata Purana, and a new story: Krishna as a child. Day eight hundred seventy-nine.
screen: `THE LAST JOURNEY ENDS.` · `A NEW BOOK OPENS.`

segments.voice: The wedding is over and the music is still playing. Devaki, a princess of the Yadu clan, has just married Vasudeva, and they are riding home together. Her cousin Kamsa, a prince of Mathura, wants to honor her, so he takes the reins himself and drives the bridal chariot. Conches, drums, gifts of horses and elephants. A happy brother on a happy day. And then, the Bhagavata says, a voice speaks out of the sky, without a body, straight at the driver. Fool, it says. The eighth child of the woman you are driving will kill you.
screen: `A WEDDING CHARIOT.` → `KAMSA HOLDS THE REINS.` → `A VOICE FROM THE SKY.`

segments.voice: Kamsa's answer is instant. He grabs his cousin by the hair and draws his sword. The wedding procession stops dead. What happens next is the first surprise of this story. Vasudeva doesn't fight. He talks. In the Bhagavata he reasons with Kamsa, gently. Death, he says, comes to everyone who is born, today or in a hundred years; killing a woman, your own sister, on her wedding day, won't change that. It will only stain you. Kamsa won't listen. So Vasudeva thinks fast, and he makes a terrible bargain to save his wife's life right now. I'll bring you every son she bears, he promises. They're the danger, not her. Kamsa knows Vasudeva keeps his word. He lowers the sword. And Vasudeva does keep it. When their first son is born, he carries the baby to Kamsa himself. The text praises him for this: a man who holds to truth even when it costs everything. Kamsa, for a moment, is moved. Only the eighth child is my danger, he says; take this one home. That moment of mercy doesn't last. The sage Narada visits Kamsa and stirs up his fear, and Kamsa locks Devaki and Vasudeva in a prison and begins to kill their children. This is how the story of Krishna's birth begins: not with a cradle, but with a promise made at sword point, and a father who keeps it. The book that will be full of a child's laughter starts in a prison cell.
screen: `THE SWORD COMES OUT` · `VASUDEVA REASONS WITH KAMSA` · `"I'LL BRING YOU EVERY SON"` · then, large: `A PROMISE KEPT, A PRISON CELL`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let your breath slow. Vasudeva's first move was not to fight but to speak calmly to someone who had a sword out. Bring to mind one tense conversation you might face this week. Breathe in, and picture yourself staying steady in it. Breathe out, and let your jaw and hands loosen. You don't need the right words yet. Just practice the steadiness. If you pray, you can ask in your own way for a calm voice. The bell holds the time.
The birth. Krishna's story starts before he is born, with a voice at a wedding and a promise Vasudeva keeps.
Your line: a promise made at sword point. Today, when something goes wrong, try speaking calmly first, the way Vasudeva did on the chariot. Day eight hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: The story of Krishna's birth is told in the tenth book of the Bhagavata Purana; Hindus hear it in recitations and festival retellings, especially around Krishna Janmashtami.

fork.setup: you're Vasudeva. your bride's cousin has a sword at her throat on your wedding day. what do you do?
options: fight him with your bare hands.
reason with him, then promise him your sons.
fork.reveal: he argues first that death comes to all, then promises every son to save Devaki's life, and he keeps the promise.

original.note: janma: birth. the Bhagavata's account of Krishna's birth begins with this wedding.

trapdoor: what you thought: Krishna's story begins in a cradle.
what it means: it begins at a wedding, with a sword drawn and a promise made to save a bride.
what a scholar hears: the Bhagavata praises Vasudeva for keeping that promise, so the story opens on truthfulness in an impossible place.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.1: the wedding of Vasudeva and Devaki, the voice from the sky, Vasudeva's reasoning and promise, the first son, Narada's visit, the imprisonment

notes: All paraphrase; the voice's words and the dialogue are glosses, not quotations from any translation.
Vasudeva's 'today or in a hundred years' follows the Bhagavata's own wording of his argument (10.1.38); confirm.

Confirm in 10.1: Kamsa drives the chariot out of affection; the bodiless voice names the eighth child; Vasudeva's argument that death is certain for the born; Kamsa's release of the first son (Kirtiman); Narada's visit prompting imprisonment.
Kamsa is called Devaki's cousin (he is the son of Ugrasena, she the daughter of Devaka, Ugrasena's brother); the text often calls her his sister. Confirm preferred wording.
